meta.title: Who really said "Do not spoil what you have by desiring what you have not"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it's Epicurus — it's Vatican Saying 35. But the familiar English is Russel M. Geer's 1964 translation, not Epicurus's literal words.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do not spoil what you have by desiring what you have not'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Epicurus — Vatican Saying 35 — but the exact wording is a 1964 translation by Russel M. Geer, and other translators word it very differently.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 341–270 BC · Greek philosopher, founder of Epicureanism
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Epicurean maxim — number 35 of the Vatican Sayings (Sententiae Vaticanae), a collection rediscovered in an 1888 Vatican Library manuscript that preserves the views of Epicurus and his immediate circle. The exact English wording you see is Russel M. Geer’s 1964 translation (Bobbs-Merrill), Vatican Saying XXXV; other translators render the Greek quite differently.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Do not spoil what you have by desiring what you have not; remember that what you now have was once among the things you only hoped for.
trail: The line is Vatican Saying 35 in the Sententiae Vaticanae ↗, a set of 81 Epicurean aphorisms found in an 1888 Vatican Library manuscript that preserves the views of Epicurus and his immediate followers.
The exact English wording is traced to Russel M. Geer’s 1964 Bobbs-Merrill translation ↗, cited as Vatican Saying XXXV, p. 68.

Other translators render the same Greek differently — Peter Saint-Andre ↗ gives “Don’t ruin the things you have by wanting what you don’t have…” — showing the familiar phrasing belongs to one translator, not to Epicurus verbatim.
source.excerptNote: Vatican Saying 35 is a standalone aphorism; the surrounding sayings in the collection turn on the same Epicurean theme — contentment with present goods and the taming of restless desire.

source.rightsNote: The ancient Greek maxim is public domain, but the exact English wording shown is Russel M. Geer’s 1964 translation, first published by Bobbs-Merrill — a post-1930 rendering by an identifiable translator and publisher, so this specific wording is treated as in-copyright. A public-domain phrasing exists in Cyril Bailey’s 1926 Oxford edition, but it reads differently (“…was the gift of fortune”).

author.name: Epicurus
author.heading: About Epicurus
author.metaLine: 341–270 BC · Greek philosopher, founder of Epicureanism
author.bio: Epicurus (341–270 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher, born on Samos, who founded the school of thought known as Epicureanism and taught in his Athens garden. He held that a pleasant, tranquil life comes from moderating desire, dispelling needless fear, and valuing friendship — the very themes behind this saying. Most of his vast output is lost; what survives comes through a few letters, the Principal Doctrines, and the Vatican Sayings.

misattribution.heading: The catch: right author, one translator's words
misattribution.intro: The good news for once: this really is Epicurus. The wrinkle is that the crisp English everyone shares is a single modern translator’s work, and the line is occasionally hung on the wrong ancient name.

items.why: The polished sentence — “…remember that what you now have was once among the things you only hoped for” — is Geer’s 1964 rendering ↗, not Epicurus’s literal words. Cyril Bailey (1926) ↗ ended it “…was the gift of fortune,” a meaningfully different reading of the same Greek.

Because Seneca quotes Epicurus constantly in his Letters to Lucilius, the line is sometimes filed under Seneca. But it does not appear in Seneca’s epistles; it is Vatican Saying 35 ↗, from the Epicurean collection itself.

items.who: Cited as if from a treatise or letter
items.why: It is a one-line maxim from the Vatican Sayings — a florilegium of aphorisms — not a passage lifted from a formal work or personal letter of Epicurus.

misattribution.truthLine: It is Epicurus — Vatican Saying 35 ↗ — but the memorable English is Russel M. Geer’s 1964 translation, one of several quite different renderings of the Greek.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: The saying compresses the core of Epicurean ethics into one sentence: our restlessness for what we lack quietly poisons the enjoyment of what we already hold. Epicurus’s remedy is memory — recalling that today’s ordinary possessions were once the very things we longed for.
It has become a staple of modern Stoic-and-Epicurean self-help feeds, usually stripped of any note that it is Vatican Saying 35 or that the English is a mid-20th-century translation.
